Meeting header:

- Duration: ~49 minutes
- Recorded: yes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE); Priya Anand (Redwood SE); Evan Park (SprintBoard VP Eng); Sophie Laurent (Platform); Tom Hsu (SRE); Aisha Khan (PM)

Summary (auto): quick discovery focused on SprintBoard's p95 latency targets, streaming use case (live chat), concurrency model and token/sec benchmarking. Customer leaning toward Hosted for velocity but has strict data residency/KMS needs for VIP customers; exploring Dedicated or Private for a pilot.

Topics: p95 targets, streaming/partial responses, concurrency at burst, token/second profiling, fallback to smaller model, SOC2/KMS audit requirements.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick roll call?
[00:04] Evan Park: Evan here.
[00:06] Sophie Laurent: Sophie.
[00:07] Tom Hsu: Tom.
[00:09] Aisha Khan: Aisha.
[00:12] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos, hi.
[00:13] Priya Anand: Priya.
[00:15] Maya Chen: great. quick agenda, we'll ask about current infra, expected p95 and concurrency, demo our routing options (hosted/dedicated/private) and then next steps re: benchmarks. sound good?
[00:24] Evan Park: yep. for context, SprintBoard runs an embedded chat assistant inside our scheduling UI. typical session is 1-3 turns but we have periodic long-form prompts when users request summary — those are up to 1,800 tokens. baseline traffic is low but we expect large spikes after marketing pushes, sometimes 220 concurrent sessions for a region for 5-10 minutes.
[00:45] Sophie Laurent: and half our customers are in EU so data residency matters, some enterprise customers require customer-managed keys.
[00:52] Maya Chen: perfect, that helps. what's your current p95 SLA target for response time? overall or for streaming?
[00:59] Evan Park: as a product, we want p95 end-to-end under 400ms for small responses (<=256 tokens) and under 1.2s for longer streaming responses, ideally. but honestly, for the marketing bursts we care more about keeping p95 under 2s and avoiding tail spikes.
[01:18] Carlos Ruiz: ok that's useful. couple clarifying q's: when you say streaming are you using partial token streaming to the client? or you accumulate then send?
[01:26] Tom Hsu: streaming — we stream token-by-token to the browser, yes. we also do optimistic rendering on the UI so latency jitter is very visible.
[01:34] Priya Anand: good to know. and how do you handle cold start? do you have background warmers?
[01:39] Sophie Laurent: currently we run a cron that pings a local model cluster but it's unreliable during big bursts. we also tried autoscaling pods but kube scale takes too long.
[01:48] Maya Chen: that lines up with a lot of customers. Redwood can offer prefix/KV cache to reduce repeated token cost and continuous batching to improve throughput; for streaming we tune batching window to keep latency SLOs while grouping requests.
[02:01] Evan Park: can you quantify that—like how much latency do you add for batching?
[02:06] Carlos Ruiz: typical batching windows are 10-30ms for low latency config, sometimes 50-100ms if you're optimizing throughput. the runtime also uses adaptive batching: if you see many short requests we keep the window small; for big bursts we slightly increase to improve GPU utilization.
[02:21] Aisha Khan: important: for our compliance team, we need KMS integration and auditable logs — SOC2 plus an eU data residency note. do you support bring-your-own-key?
[02:31] Priya Anand: yes, Private and Dedicated options support customer-managed KMS and we have audit logs; Hosted can be configured with SMB key options but for full BYOK you'd look at Private. we'll share the security pack after NDA.
[02:43] Sophie Laurent: good. on the Dedicated side we care about predictable throughput. what does throughput look like for say a 13B open model on common GPU types?
[02:53] Carlos Ruiz: rough numbers: with a 13B unquantized on an A100-ish profile you might see ~250-350 tokens/sec sustained per GPU depending on seq len; on an H100 it's higher. quantized int8 paths can get 2-3x depending on quality tradeoffs. for streaming p95 we usually recommend profiling with your real prompts because sequence length distribution matters a lot.
[03:14] Evan Park: we run a lot of short prompts and occasional 1.8k token summaries, so distribution is bimodal. how do you handle long KV cache across streaming sessions?
[03:24] Priya Anand: Redwood's KV cache persists prefixes for the session and we can pin longer contexts on Dedicated/Private; on Hosted we provide session-level TTL controls. caching reduces repeated compute for common system prompts, etc.
[03:34] Tom Hsu: ok. let's talk concurrency — when you say GPU supports X tokens/sec, how does that map to concurrent sessions if half are streaming and half are short? we need a capacity formula.
[03:44] Carlos Ruiz: good q. we usually recommend building a traffic mix: e.g., 70% short (<256 tokens, median 120 tokens) and 30% long (average 1200 tokens). then simulate. For rough math: if a GPU does 300 tokens/sec and short sessions average 120 tokens, that's ~2.5 short completions/sec, so about 150 short sessions completed per minute, but streaming ties up a slot longer. we provide a simulator and a spreadsheet — we'll run it against your traces.
[04:11] Sophie Laurent: can we do a firehose replay? we can give a 1-hour trace next week.
[04:15] Maya Chen: yes please, that's ideal. Carlos will prepare the benchmark harness to replay at different QPS and concurrency.
[04:21] Evan Park: what's the typical p95 for streaming with partial token flush with Redwood's low-latency mode?
[04:28] Carlos Ruiz: in low-latency mode with small batch windows and an H100 profile, we see streaming token latencies in p95 often sub-200ms for short tokens; end-to-end including network depends on your infra but from runtime perspective 150-300ms p95 token flush is common. again that depends on kernel selection and seq len.
[04:48] Aisha Khan: we have customers that require 99.9% availability and we want graceful degradation. what's your fallback story when capacity hits?
[04:57] Priya Anand: Redwood has automated fallback routing: if a primary model or region is saturated, requests can route to a cheaper smaller model, or to an async queue depending on policy. you can configure per-route SLOs and fallback hierarchy.
[05:08] Sophie Laurent: do you support multi-region active-active? we want EU failover to remain in EU.
[05:12] Maya Chen: yes, smart routing by region is supported; for strict data residency we route only to EU zones or to Private.
[05:19] Evan Park: what about cold-start due to KV cache eviction during a burst? we've seen latency cliffs when cache is cold.
[05:27] Carlos Ruiz: caching eviction policies are tunable. for Dedicated/Private you can provision more memory for KV state or pin hot sessions. for Hosted we have a cache tier that attempts to keep hot prefixes in memory and pre-warm during scheduled campaigns.
[05:41] Tom Hsu: can the runtime pre-warm on a schedule? we do predictable marketing sends.
[05:44] Priya Anand: yes, you can schedule warmers or run pre-warm load ahead of campaign windows; Redwood also supports warm pools for Dedicated.
[05:53] Sophie Laurent: let's get specific on a benchmark. we want p95 end-to-end under 1.2s for most cases, and under 2s for marketing bursts. can you run a token/sec bench that replays our mixture (70/30 short/long) and show p95 and throughput at 1) Hosted low-latency config, 2) Dedicated 1 GPU per 8 capacity (example), 3) Private on local rack?
[06:12] Carlos Ruiz: yep that's doable. timeline wise: if you can share trace and sample prompts we'll run a 2-pass test: functional replay for correctness and then full throughput sweeps. we can include configurations for kernel/quantization and for batching windows.
[06:25] Evan Park: pricing question — how much more is Dedicated vs Hosted for predictable performance?
[06:29] Maya Chen: high level: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated has a monthly reservation plus utilization—usually more economical at steady high QPS and gives you reserved capacity. Private has platform fees and one-time setup. i'll send a pricing matrix but concrete numbers depend on model size and commit.
[06:45] Aisha Khan: also, for Private we need air-gapped install docs and support SLAs. is that on the table?
[06:51] Priya Anand: yes we have an on-prem package with offline installer and support tiers; will include SSO/SAML and HSM integrations.
[06:58] Tom Hsu: technical deep dive — does Redwood support per-request routing keys so we can steer enterprise customers to Private clusters?
[07:05] Carlos Ruiz: yes, routing policy allows per-tenant rules. you can pin customer X to Private and route others to Hosted.
[07:11] Sophie Laurent: any gotchas for streaming web sockets? we use websockets with chunked tokens, do you have a recommended pattern?
[07:18] Priya Anand: we recommend server-side backpressure and token-chunking at ~256 token boundaries for UX; Redwood supports websocket streaming and has examples in the SDK. we'll share sample code.
[07:28] Evan Park: one of our internal concerns: tokenization differences across models—if you fallback to a smaller model the token count changes and could change billing and latency — how do you handle that?
[07:37] Carlos Ruiz: good point. fallbacks change model behavior; we expose token accounting per model and show delta estimates before fallback. you can also disable fallback for certain customer routes.
[07:47] Maya Chen: quick check: Sophie, Tom, what does your observability look like today? do you have per-token metrics?
[07:55] Sophie Laurent: our telemetry is basic—request/response times, and we log total tokens but not per-token latency.
[08:01] Carlos Ruiz: Redwood gives per-request token breakdowns, p95 per model, and token-level traces if you enable extended retention — helpful for regressions.
[08:10] Aisha Khan: for the benchmark, we need the output artifacts to prove to SRE — p95, p99, throughput, GPU utilization, and a runbook for failure modes.
[08:18] Priya Anand: will include all that.
[08:21] Evan Park: timeline — can you do an initial bench by 2026-04-30 if we provide traces tomorrow?
[08:26] Carlos Ruiz: probably tight but we can do an initial replay and quick numbers by 04-30; full sweeps by 05-05.
[08:32] Sophie Laurent: that's fine.
[08:34] Maya Chen: ok recap and next steps: Carlos to share benchmark harness and sample config; Sophie to upload 1-hour trace and representative prompts; Maya to share pricing and security pack after NDA; schedule pilot kick-off for week of 2026-05-04.
[08:47] Evan Park: one more thing — do you have references that did streaming p95 tuning?
[08:51] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share a short case study (anonymized) of a customer that lowered p95 from 1.2s to 350ms for short tokens using caching + batching tuning.
[08:59] Aisha Khan: please include your SOC2 scope page and KMS integration notes.
[09:04] Priya Anand: will do.
[09:07] Tom Hsu: thanks, that was useful.
[09:09] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of meeting.
